design_detail: Critical narrative review (Annual Review of Psychology 76:143-165; read as the NIH author manuscript in PMC) of the therapeutic evidence for ketamine, MDMA, psilocybin and LSD, by four addiction and drug-policy researchers (Stanford/VA, Oregon Health & Science University, University of Queensland). No search strategy; explicit minimum standard for the evidence discussed: randomized trials in people with diagnosed disorders with more than 15 participants per condition. For MDMA only the two phase 3 PTSD trials meet it. Includes 'warnings to the wise' boxes on hype, bias and money, a section on mechanisms, and a policy section on regulation, including Australia's 2023 decision. No retracted source is cited.
can_establish: What a critical review applying a minimum standard concludes about the therapeutic evidence for MDMA and other psychedelics, which MDMA trials meet that standard, and which design weaknesses (blinding, expectancy, enrolment, follow-up) it identifies.
cannot_establish: Completeness (no systematic search), the size of any effect (no pooling), or anything about MDMA for indications other than PTSD, for which no trial met the standard and none is discussed.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). The evidence for MDMA comprises the two phase 3 trials (Mitchell et al., 2021, 2023).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Randomized controlled trials of people with diagnosed disorders with more than 15 participants in each condition; open-label trials and trials with failed or unassessed blinding included with cautions; claims about consciousness, creativity or social goals excluded; ayahuasca, mescaline, ibogaine and DMT judged to lack enough high-quality evidence to review (Minimal research quality standards imposed in this review, 3rd paragraph; Definitions and Scope, 3rd and 4th paragraphs).
sample.selection_effects: Selection by the authors under a stated threshold, without a search; the threshold excludes all MDMA studies outside the two phase 3 PTSD trials.

exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: As described for the first phase 3 trial: three sessions of MDMA (80 to 180 mg per session) 4 weeks apart (study conditions as reported by the review).

analysis.effect_sizes: None computed; results described in words, with the MAPP2 blinding figures and severe adverse event percentages.
analysis.selective_reporting: The review discusses only trials meeting its threshold, by design.
analysis.power: Not applicable; the authors argue that meta-analyses of very small trials inflate effects.

interpretation_gap.results_show: For MDMA, two sponsor-run phase 3 trials found larger falls in PTSD scores than placebo with the same therapy; blinding was not tested in the first, failed in the second, and expectancy may account for some or all of the difference; severe adverse events were more frequent on MDMA in the second.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The review concludes that MDMA for PTSD is a positive signal that warrants replication in stronger studies and should not be taken as definitive. This is consistent with its own appraisal. Its prediction that approval was likely was overtaken before print (see reporting issues), and its policy section states predictions as near-certainties.

timeline.event: Burke and Blumberger's commentary raises the expectancy concern that this review cites.
Second phase 3 trial (MAPP2), the first with a blinding survey.
13 August 2024: the BMJ reports the FDA's rejection of the application and three retractions (Mahase, 2024); this review, published online in December 2024, still predicts approval.

replication.where_it_stands: A critical narrative review that may be cited for its argument and its threshold-based finding that only the two phase 3 PTSD trials qualified for MDMA; claims resting only on it stay at draft (METHODS §6.3).

funding.funder: Acknowledgements: Keith Humphreys, Esther Ting Memorial Professorship and grants from the Department of Veterans Affairs, the National Institute on Drug Abuse and the Wu Tsai Neurosciences Institute; Todd Korthuis, NIDA grant UG1DA015815; Wayne Hall, emeritus professor at a centre with core funding from the Australian Commonwealth Department of Health.
funding.declared_conflicts: Not reported in the author manuscript (no disclosure statement printed).
funding.affiliations_note: The authors are addiction and drug-policy researchers who have written critically about medical cannabis; their own papers are cited for the policy arguments, not for the efficacy evidence.

what_would_settle_it: Adequately powered, independently run trials of MDMA-assisted therapy with active placebos, measured expectancy and blinding, representative participants (fewer with prior psychedelic experience) and long-term follow-up, in PTSD and in any other proposed indication.

domains.note: Explicit, reproducible threshold for the evidence discussed, but no search strategy, databases or dates.
Each trial discussed is appraised for blinding, sample size, comparator, expectancy and follow-up.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: The authors' own work is cited for arguments about hype and policy, not for the efficacy evidence.

The evidence sections are cautious, but the policy section states predictions as near-certainties (post-approval practice will resemble the medical cannabis industry) and attributes Australia's decision to lobbying without cited evidence.

domains.domain: Balance of the case for and against efficacy (the trialists' replies to the expectancy critique are not presented)
domains.note: The positive trial results are reported, but counter-arguments from the trialists are not; the review is avowedly sceptical.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to narrative reviews (METHODS §5.3). This is a careful critical review with an explicit threshold, useful for its appraisal of design weaknesses and for the observation that, for MDMA, only the two sponsor-run PTSD phase 3 trials met a modest standard. It is not a systematic synthesis and gives no effect sizes; claims citing it alone stay at draft.

key_findings.finding: Minimum standard for the evidence discussed: randomized controlled trials of people with diagnosed disorders, with more than 15 participants in each condition; open-label trials and trials whose blinding was not assessed or failed are discussed with cautions.
key_findings.locator: Minimal research quality standards imposed in this review, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: As an illustration of the evidence base, Kisely et al.'s (2023) meta-analysis of psilocybin and MDMA screened 837 studies and found 14 randomized trials, only one with at least 30 participants and none demonstrating successful blinding.
key_findings.locator: Minimal research quality standards imposed in this review, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: For MDMA the review discusses only the two phase 3 PTSD trials, run by a consortium assembled and funded by MAPS, which the review calls an advocacy organization; no MDMA trial in another indication meets its standard.
key_findings.locator: Safety and Effectiveness of Psychedelic Drugs › MDMA for post-traumatic stress disorder, 1st paragraph; Definitions and Scope, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: First trial: the mean CAPS-5 change was significantly larger with MDMA, but blinding was not formally tested; the trial's argument that at least 10% guessed their arm wrongly implies that up to 90% could have guessed it, which raises the concern that expectancy biased the results (citing Burke and Blumberger, 2021; Flameling et al., 2023).
key_findings.locator: MDMA for post-traumatic stress disorder, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Second trial (53 MDMA, 51 placebo): severe adverse events in 9.4% on MDMA against 3.9% on placebo; large decreases in CAPS-5 in both groups, larger with MDMA; blinding assessed formally: 75% on placebo and 94.2% on MDMA correctly guessed their assignment, so expectancy may account for some or all of the difference; an ICER report argued that enrolment may have been skewed toward people with strong faith in MDMA.
key_findings.locator: MDMA for post-traumatic stress disorder, 4th paragraph
key_findings.note: 'Severe' refers to graded severity, not to serious adverse events.

key_findings.finding: Summary: MDMA for PTSD is one of the positive signals; because of absent successful blinding and likely expectancy effects, none of these signals should be taken as definitive without replication in methodologically stronger studies, all of which warrant such replication.
key_findings.locator: Summary of Effectiveness Evidence for Psychedelic Medicines, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: On dependence: apart from ketamine and perhaps MDMA, psychedelic drugs do not seem to have significant addictive liability; MDMA is described as possibly addictive.
key_findings.locator: Definitions and Scope, 1st paragraph; Word to the Wise #5 (box)

key_findings.finding: Australia's Therapeutic Goods Administration in 2023 allowed authorized psychiatrists to prescribe MDMA for PTSD (and psilocybin for intractable depression) under its Special Access Scheme, a decision the review says went against the advice of the TGA's own expert panel and was opposed by the Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists and the Australian Psychological Society.
key_findings.locator: Policy Implications › Australia as a case study in regulatory failure, 1st and 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Research priorities: better blinding with assessment and reporting of expectancy and blinding in every trial; more representative participants (about half of trial patients have used psychedelics, against about 10% of the general population, per Nayak et al., 2023, and Krebs and Johansen, 2013); longer follow-ups.

reporting_issues.issue: The MDMA section predicts that FDA approval was likely in the near future; the FDA had rejected the application by 13 August 2024, when the BMJ reported it (mahase_2024), months before this review was published online (December 2024) and in print (January 2025), and the text was not updated.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (MDMA for post-traumatic stress disorder, 5th paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: The regulatory statement is outdated; it does not affect the appraisal of the trials.

reporting_issues.issue: The first trial's therapy is described as 3 hours of manualized therapy before the first dose and three weekly 90-minute sessions after each dosing session; the trial report, as carded by the project, describes three 90-minute preparatory sessions and three 90-minute integration sessions after each experimental session (sc_mitchell_2021).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (MDMA for post-traumatic stress disorder, 2nd paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor second-hand inaccuracy; cite the trial report for the design.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC11890197 (NIH author manuscript NIHMS2055935 of the Annual Review of Psychology article; all sections, boxes, acknowledgements and reference list; no figures or tables). Crossref record read in this reader's tab.
